6.0.s.en: 1. The sufferer has the right to complain

6.0.0.en: 1 Then Job answered and said: 2 Oh that my grief were weighed, and my calamity lifted into all the balances together! 3 For now it is heavier than the sand of the sea: therefore my words are rash. 4 For the arrows of the Almighty are within me, the poison whereof drinketh up my spirit: the terrors of God do set themselves in array against me. 5 Doth the wild ass bray when he hath grass? or loweth the ox over his fodder? 6 Can that which is unsavoury be eaten without salt? or is there any taste in the broth of the herb? 7 The things that my soul refused to touch, these have become as my loathsome bread!

6.0.2.en: Although the one who entered into the dialogue with him was Eliphaz, Job realized that Eliphaz was speaking in the name of all together, so Job directed his answer to all (Job 15:5).

6.0.3.en: Job was marked by prudence and composure, for he did not interrupt Eliphaz, who began his speech harshly. And Job listened patiently until Eliphaz had finished all he wished to say.

6.1.0.en: Oh that my grief were weighed, and my calamity lifted into all the balances together [2].

6.1.1.en: Job disclosed his grief, that it cannot be fully depicted nor fully comprehended by anyone. And there is no balance in the world that can weigh his sorrow, so he asked that all the balances be gathered to weigh his intense sorrow.

6.1.2.en: * [Then Job answered and said: Ah, who will truly weigh my grief, and lift my calamity into all the balances?] This statement concerns the former words (Job 3:4-5): "Thou hast instructed many... and thou hast strengthened the feeble knees. But now it is come upon thee, and thou faintest; it toucheth thee, and thou art troubled."

6.1.3.en: I would that my affliction be made clear, and that you realize that no one has experienced such sorrows. Look at my calamity, for by its nature it makes an excuse for me, even though, strictly speaking, what concerns me is a thing that cannot be forgiven...

6.1.4.en: Eliphaz proved that this calamity is due to his wickedness, presenting the argument for it: "Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished, being innocent? or where were the upright cut off?" (Job 4:7). He speaks exactly as the barbarians spoke about Paul after the viper bit him in Malta: "Whom, though he hath escaped the sea, justice suffereth not to live" (Acts 4:28).

6.1.5.en: He says: Men - especially the common people - judge events in a naive, random way; they do not base their judgments on a person's conduct, but rather on the disciplines and punishments that befall him. Therefore Eliphaz says: [Shall mortal man (the human being) be more just than God?] (Job 4:17). Job answers: I cannot answer, nor say that I suffer such many and terrifying sorrows without having committed any sin, for the blows speak against me. He says: I am able to approach the Almighty and wrestle with Him.

6.1.6.en: St. John Chrysostom * Who is given the title "balances" but the Mediator between God and man, who came to weigh the merit of our life and to bring down with Him both justice and tenderness together?

6.2.0.en: For now it is heavier than the sand of the sea: therefore my words are rash [3].

6.2.1.en: His calamities were multiplied and exceedingly heavy, so that they could be neither counted nor weighed, for they are "heavier than the sand of the sea." Therefore he asked that excuse be sought for him if [his words were rash], that is, if anything in them seemed vain or mixed with bitterness, for amid these pains it is hard to adorn words or even to control them.

6.2.2.en: Thus Job apologizes for the furious expressions that came from his mouth when he cursed the day of his conception or his birth. He does not justify this, but he expected his friends to take his state into account before criticizing him. It was fitting for them to treat him gently amid the terror of his calamity, for he needs tenderness, not bitter criticism.

6.2.3.en: * If you put my grief in a balance, my judgments together with the torments of my sufferings, and weigh them, not separately but all together, you will find my sorrows "heavier than the sand of the sea." For what grieved Job was not the loss of his possessions, nor the loss of his wealth, nor the crushing of his children, nor the pus issuing from his sores, but the painful results to which his spirit had come... All the visible waves of the sea are not as heavy as the words that come forth with the destruction issuing from the enemy's interruption.

6.3.0.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem For the arrows of the Almighty are within me, the poison whereof drinketh up my spirit (my spirit drinks their poison): the terrors of God do set themselves in array against me [4].

6.3.1.en: What are the arrows of the Almighty that are aimed at the children of God, so that they drink up their spirit? They are the arrows of love which God aims at His saints, so they are wounded with divine love, and long for death that they may meet with Him and experience His divine love in its most perfect form.

6.3.2.en: Many of the Fathers see that the Father, in His love for mankind, aimed His precious arrow, the Word of God, driving it toward the hearts of men to wound them with the wounds of love, so that the soul cries out: [I am wounded with love] (Song 5:2).

6.3.3.en: And as God aims the arrows of His love at our hearts to grant them the wounds of love that bring healing and happiness on an eternal level, so the enemy of good hurls his arrows kindled with fire into the hearts of men in order to kill them and make them fit for eternal Gehenna (Eph 6:16).

6.3.4.en: This image is surely taken from a common custom among barbarian nations, who dip the heads of arrows in poisonous substances, so that when they strike anyone they carry him off to death.

6.3.5.en: If the calamities that befell him cannot be weighed by any balances, what is more serious than that is the inner arrows, the arrows of the Almighty that were aimed at him. He sees God, whom he loves and worships, having brought these troubles upon him and aimed His arrows at him.

6.3.6.en: He felt as if their poison, or the venom with which the arrows were anointed, had seeped into his spirit, so that he lost his balance and his depths collapsed.

6.3.7.en: He stood astonished. He is in a battle before the army of God drawn up against him; God fights him with His terrors, so from where can he have consolation? He cannot lift his eyes to heaven, for he finds no consolations coming down upon him from it, but the terrors of God resist him.

6.3.8.en: * The bride praised the spear-thrower for his accurate aim, because he struck her with his arrow. So the bride said: "I am wounded (sick) with love" (Song 5:2). These words mean that the arrows of the Bridegroom have penetrated into her heart. The One who aims these arrows is Love (1 Jn 4:8), who sends [his chosen arrow] (Isa 49:2), the only-begotten Son, to those who are being saved, and then dips the point of the three-pointed arrow in the spirit of life. The point of the arrow is faith, and through it God presents the Archer and the arrow together to the heart, as the Lord Christ says: "If a man love me, he will keep my words: and my Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him" (Jn 23:14).

6.3.9.en: Fr. Gregory of Nyssa * The soul that has risen to the high divine degrees sees within itself the sweet arrow of love that wounded it, and boasts of this wound, saying: "I am wounded with love." O beautiful wound and sweet arrow that brought life into my heart! For the penetration of the arrow opened a door and an entrance for love, which is the imaginary transformation from the shooting of arrows to the joy of the wedding. St. Job points to those arrows, and when he suffered his intense pains he declared that the arrows of the Lord had pierced him (Job 6:4). Truly we usually look upon the arrows as the words of God. But could he feel many pains when he was pierced by them?

6.3.10.en: The words of God, though they are arrows, arouse love, not pain. Or are they arrows because there is no love without pain? When we love something without possessing it we cannot help but feel sorrow. A man loves without pain when he possesses the object of his love, and then he neither suffers nor groans. Therefore the bride of Christ in the person of the Church speaks these words in the Song of Songs: [For I am wounded with love] (Song 2:5; 5:8). She declares herself wounded with love. She loves what she has not yet attained, she grieves because she has not yet possessed it. And since she grieves she is wounded, but this wound quickly brings her to perfect true health. He who is not struck by this wound will not be able to reach perfect true health.

6.3.11.en: * [For thine arrows stick fast in me, and thy hand presseth me sore] (Ps 2:38)... The same punishment (that was on Adam), the same wrath, that is, the pains of both mind and body, is a necessity we must bear here, which he described as "arrows." And Job referred to the same arrows (Job 4:6), and said that the arrows of righteousness were fixed in him, while he suffered under those pains.

6.3.12.en: We have also been accustomed to call the words of God arrows, as those that give love, not pain... Let us then understand "thine arrows stick fast" thus: "Thy words are fixed in my heart."

6.3.13.en: By these very words it happens that I remember the Sabbath, and by remembering the Sabbath (eternity) and not yet having attained it, I am deprived of joy in the present time, and I remember that I have no health in my body, nor is it fitting for me to reckon it health when I compare it with the health I shall receive in eternal rest, when this corruptible shall put on incorruption, and this mortal shall put on immortality (1 Cor 53:15), and I see by comparison with what I shall be that the present health is nothing but sickness.

6.3.14.en: St. Augustine * It pierces me in this way, not merely shot into my body, but it has deprived me of balanced judgment.

6.3.15.en: St. John Chrysostom * [For the arrows of the Lord are in my body, their violence drinketh up my blood; whenever I wish to speak, they pierce me] (Job 6:4). Job was crushed by these arrows. This is what David sang in the Psalms: [For thine arrows stick fast in me, and thy hand presseth me sore] (Ps 2:38). For both speak of sorrows which enemies aim against them by God's permission, and for this reason Job says: [Their violence drinketh up my blood]. As if he says: The riches of my soul have been drained; I cannot stand in the face of those who corrupt me with a blazing face. For when Job begins to speak, the pains pierce him. Especially when the speech is long, his wounds appear with greater force, so he puts a bridle to keep his words in check, lest they not entirely please God.

6.4.0.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Doth the wild ass bray when he hath grass? or loweth the ox over his fodder? [5]

6.4.1.en: Instead of criticizing him, it was fitting for them to share his sufferings, for his complaint and the bitterness of his soul are not without cause; the irrational animals do not cry out without reason.

6.4.2.en: Job expressed the state of weakness he had reached because of the multitude and severity of the calamities and the element of surprise, besides his friends' indifference to his state, for instead of offering a word of consolation to support him, they began to heap many serious accusations upon him.

6.4.3.en: He became like a stone without feeling, unable to express what is within him; he cannot bray like the wild ass because he finds no grass, nor low (cry out) like the ox over his fodder. He was forced to eat food unfit for him as a man without opening his mouth.

6.4.4.en: He came into a position not to be envied, for he knows he cannot be justified before God, but he was awaiting words of consolation from his companions that would open before his shattered soul the doors of hope, and not that despair should shatter him.

6.4.5.en: Pope Gregory sees that he became as one who had fallen under the curse of the Law that exposes sin, without grace extending to him to raise him. Truly there is no fault in the Law, but there is a need for the grace that forgives sins, which the Law exposed. It was fitting for Job's friends to support him by looking to the grace of God, not to rebuke him bitterly and shatter his soul.

6.4.6.en: * Can anyone taste what brings death by tasting it? For he who tastes the Law in a carnal manner brings death, since its commandment shows sin and does not remove it... as Paul testifies, saying: "For the law made nothing perfect" (Heb 19:7). And also: "Wherefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good" (Rom 12:7-13), and then immediately he says: "But sin, that it might appear sin, working death in me by that which is good; that sin by the commandment might become exceeding sinful" (Rom 13:7)

6.4.8.en: * The commandments of Moses are "the ministration of condemnation," while grace through the Savior he calls "the ministration of righteousness," which exceeds in glory...

6.4.9.en: The Law that condemns was given by Moses, but the grace that justifies came through the only-begotten Son. How then is Christ not surpassingly glorious beyond all comparison?

6.4.10.en: St. Cyril the Great * The Law condemns sinners, but grace receives them and justifies them by faith. It leads them to holy Baptism and grants them forgiveness of sins.

6.4.11.en: Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus * The Jews are still at Marah by the bitter waters, because God has not yet shown them the tree by which the water becomes sweet.

6.4.12.en: * The Lord cast a tree into the waters, which made them sweet. But when the tree (cross) of Jesus comes, and the teaching of my Savior dwells within me, then the law of Moses becomes "sweet," and its taste, to him who reads and understands it, becomes truly sweet".

6.5.0.en: Origen Can that which is unsavoury be eaten without salt? or is there any taste in the broth of the herb? [6]

6.5.1.en: Job was salt that, by the Lord's grace and by his surpassing love, removed corruption from many, offering them true heavenly consolations, and now that he has entered the crucible of trials, no one offered him salt. He became utterly poor materially, and in his poverty he found no salt with which to season the tasteless food that some gave him in charity.

6.5.2.en: * [Can loathsome food be eaten without salt?] (Job 6:6) In the Law the hidden meaning is the salt of the letter. He who relies on carnal observances and refuses to understand the spiritual meaning, what does he do but eat loathsome food? But this salt, that is, the truth, is put into the food when you learn that the fragrance of the hidden meaning is found in the depths of the Law, saying: "For had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me" (Jn 46:5). And also: "Have salt in yourselves, and have peace one with another" (Mk 50:9).

6.6.0.en: The things that my soul refused to touch, these have become as my loathsome bread! [7]

6.6.1.en: What his soul loathed in his days of prosperity, and what he was unable to touch with his hand, became his loathsome bread. The psalmist says: "My tears have been my meat day and night, while they continually say unto me, Where is thy God?" (Ps 42:3). "Thou feedest them with the bread of tears; and givest them tears to drink in great measure" (Ps 80:5). "For I have eaten ashes like bread, and mingled my drink with weeping" (Ps 102:9). "And the LORD said, Even thus shall the children of Israel eat their defiled bread among the Gentiles, whither I will drive them" (Ezek 4:13). As it was also said: "Say unto the people of the land, Thus saith the Lord GOD of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and of the land of Israel; They shall eat their bread with carefulness, and drink their water with astonishment, that her land may be desolate from all that is therein, because of the violence of all them that dwell therein" (Ezek 12:19). "Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD" (Amos 8:11).

6.6.2.en: * "The things that my soul refused to touch, these have become as my loathsome bread" (Job 7:6). Formerly the soul was concerned only with what was to its own benefit, disgusted at bearing the burdens of others, with little sympathy for others, and it was unable to face its opponents. Now it obliges itself to bear the weakness of its neighbor. It needs strength to overcome the opponent, so that through love of the truth it seeks the troubles of the present life with such great courage, even the things from which it formerly fled in its weakness. For by stooping (for the sake of others) it is built up. By being drawn to others it extends forward, and by sharing feelings it is strengthened, and as it opens itself to love of its neighbor, it is as if by the resolve of its determination it rises toward its Creator.

6.6.4.en: * In the same way, as the wild ass does not choose to bray without cause, nor the ox to low at the manger, so no one chooses to eat bread without salt, nor to listen to vain words. In truth he presented examples that are altogether impossible.

6.6.5.en: He says thus: I would not have chosen to lament over this matter had there not been a necessity urging me to it. If it is not acceptable to eat bread without salt, then it is no less so that I should be bound to lament and suffer pain and utter excessive words...

6.6.6.en: [For my soul finds no rest], why? Because I know that my food has a smell that the soul loathes like the smell of a lion.

6.6.7.en: The sores and pus were not enough, so he added a new torment.

6.6.8.en: The sickness had corrupted all his senses so that food became torment to him.

6.6.9.en: He says that nausea with the foul smell of gangrene removed his sensory discernment. What is more tormenting than this? Sleep gives no rest and food does not nourish him!

6.7.s.en: 2. Death is the end of troubles

6.7.0.en: 8 Oh that my request might come, and that God would grant me my hope! 9 That it would please God to crush me, and let loose his hand and cut me off. 10 Then my comfort and my rejoicing shall still be in torment that spareth not, for I have not denied the words of the Holy One. 11 What is my strength, that I should wait? and what is mine end, that I should be patient? 12 Is my strength the strength of stones? or is my flesh of brass? 13 Verily my help is not in me, and succour is driven quite from me!

6.7.1.en: Oh that my request might come, and that God would grant me my hope! [8]

6.7.2.en: Eliphaz rebuked Job harshly for seeking death, and instead of withdrawing what he had said, Job returned to repeat it more than before, and the Book has recorded his words for us, not that we may imitate him, but to warn us.

6.7.3.en: He asked God to fulfill his request and grant him his hope, not by bringing him through the trial, but by showing him mercy with death.

6.8.0.en: That it would please God to crush me, and let loose his hand and cut me off [9].

6.8.1.en: What Job hopes for in his distress is that God, who stretched out His hand against him so that he became poor and then bereaved and sick, would stretch out His hand all the more and crush him and take his life. Yet he never thought of suicide, unlike the philosopher Seneca, who encouraged suicide as a legitimate means to be rid of unbearable pains, which shows no respect for the law of God or the law of nature.

6.8.2.en: Job longed for the speed of his death, and turned this desire into a request he presented to God, but it was a prayer or request not according to God's will.

6.9.0.en: Then my comfort and my rejoicing shall still be in torment that spareth not, for I have not denied the words of the Holy One [10].

6.9.1.en: With his intense desire to be delivered from pain by death, Job's heart bore spiritual touches, so in faith he anticipates enjoying consolation and joy after his departure from the world. It is clear that Job had a good conscience and a living hope in eternity, though he expected a painful torment to overtake him before his death: "my rejoicing in torment that spareth not."

6.9.2.en: "That spareth not" or "let him not spare," as if he says: "I do not seek that God should spare me, but let Him allow the pains of death that put an end to my pains and bring me into rest.

6.9.3.en: In unseemly boldness Job challenges the Lord God and says: [Let him not spare!]

6.9.4.en: Job mixed his reproach - even if he transgressed the limits - with his faith and clinging to God's word, saying: "I have not denied (concealed) the words of the Holy One." He counted himself entrusted with the word of the holy God, perhaps having enjoyed divine visions. As if he says with the Apostle Paul that he did not receive the grace of God in vain (2 Cor 6:1). He was ready to enjoy the divine Word and to bear witness to it to others, that they might enjoy it with him.

6.9.5.en: The rule of his life is the word of the Holy One; he was not ashamed of it, nor slack in bearing witness to it.

6.9.6.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh sees that not even death can keep him from closing his mouth from witnessing and praising God.

6.9.7.en: * O Lord, I will not cease from praising You, even after my death.

6.9.8.en: He who lives for You and by You does not die; and the silence of death has no power to silence him.

6.9.9.en: Then let Him speak by my mouth, that it may be repeated after my death in the future.

6.9.10.en: * You are the Word who gives a word to those who speak; by You all who speak, speak for Your sake.

6.9.11.en: A ray, a radiance and a great light shone in me, that I may look upon You.

6.9.12.en: For by looking upon You the soul is enlightened, and so acquires goodness.

6.9.13.en: And when the soul draws away from You it is filled with darkness, and if it gazes upon You it puts on light to utter words of Your tidings...

6.9.14.en: Silence and speech stand over me demanding of me.

6.9.15.en: O Lord, order my life as You will.

6.9.16.en: If I am silent I am amazed, for I feel my insufficiency in (speech).

6.9.17.en: I am silent in amazement, and not in vain arrogance.

6.9.18.en: And if I speak, may my word be according to Your glory and for Your sake.

6.9.19.en: When the soul is filled with silence in amazement at You, this silence is speech full of every benefit. And if the soul is moved to glorify You with love... then in love I am moved, and I am moved to glorify You. And in amazement I am silent and do not cease from glorifying You.

6.9.20.en: Grant me, O Lord, amazement (in silence) and the word, that I may be enriched. Every day may I be amazed, and every day may I be moved to speak!

6.9.21.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh * He says: Surely I am not presenting to You anything contradictory. For I have no conscience drawn to resemble these things that You speak. In simplicity I say that I am enduring disciplines that exceed the limits of nature, for the trials that have befallen me exceed the capacity of the human body... He did not say: "I have passed through sufferings though I am righteous," but says that he cannot bear them, as David says: [Have mercy upon me, O LORD; for I am weak] (Ps 2:6).

6.9.22.en: St. John Chrysostom * "I have not denied the words of the Holy One." Often God's words to us are not sounds of words but works imposed on us. For He speaks to us by the things He does with us in silence. Therefore blessed Job would have denied the words of God if he had murmured at the blows upon him. But his feelings toward the one who smote him appear in his calling him "the Holy One," submissive to him who strikes him.

6.9.23.en: * "I do not deny the words of the Holy One." He never murmured at the injustice of him who smote him. For in the midst of his blows he calls the smiter "the Holy One." But we must realize that sometimes the adversary smites us with sorrows, and sometimes God does so...

6.9.24.en: By the blows of the adversary we steal away virtue, and when our evil habits are broken by the blows of the Lord we become strong in virtue.

6.9.25.en: The prophet foresaw this blow when he said: [Thou shalt shepherd them with a rod of iron, and like a potter's vessel thou shalt crush them] (Ps 9:2). For the Lord shepherds us and breaks us with a rod of iron, with the strong staff of righteousness according to His dispensation, while He gives us life from within, He grieves us from without. For He lowers the strength of the body and exalts the aim of the spirit.

6.9.26.en: Thus this blow is likened to a potter's vessel, as Paul says: [We have this treasure in earthen vessels] (2 Cor 4:7). And he describes the breaking together with the shepherding, saying: "Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day" (2 Cor 16:4). May the holy man who longs to draw near to God declare it powerfully in a spirit of humility even through the blows that befall him.

6.9.28.en: * He declares plainly: [I do not slander my holy God]. This means: I do not care for this life, I do not fear departure from this body, for I do not wish to be found a liar in relation to the testimonies that the holy God gave concerning me (Job 1:1; 2:3). For God does not bear witness to anyone's holiness except to those whom He finds practicing the works of the saints. He also said: [There is none like Job on the earth] (Job 1:8; 2:3). Therefore we must be careful during this corruptible life, since it is not possible for carnal men to receive such an important testimony from God and in the same character.

6.9.29.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem What is my strength, that I should wait?

6.10.0.en: and what is mine end, that I should be patient? [11]

6.10.1.en: Job had no hope of seeing good days again, for his health had reached the bottom, and he came to a hopeless state. There is no longer any healing for his body, and he no longer has strength to wait. Job realized how weak he had become, and it was fitting for him to put his hope in Him who bears our weakness instead of longing for death out of despair.

6.10.2.en: * [What is my strength, that I should endure? and what is mine end, that my soul should be calm?] My life is short (Job 5:14); how many cycles of months and years does it contain? How should I not be troubled over this swiftly passing life?

6.10.3.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * The Lord (Christ) had pity on his (Adam's) weakness, and entered to accept shame in his place!

6.10.4.en: * O Light of Christ, who enlightens darkened eyes, let Your light shine on my weakness, that I may be enlightened by You.

6.10.5.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh * Let us put on our heads the helmet of salvation, that we may not be wounded and die in the battle. Let us gird our loins with truth, that we may not be found weak in the fight.

6.10.6.en: Let us rise and awaken Christ, that He may calm the waves for us.

6.10.7.en: Let us take the shield against the wicked one, as the preparation of the gospel of our Savior (Eph 6:15-16).

6.10.8.en: Let us receive from our Lord authority to tread on serpents and scorpions (Lk 10:19)...

6.10.9.en: Let us rejoice in our hope at all times (Rom 12:12), that He who is our hope and Savior may rejoice in us...

6.10.10.en: Let us take for ourselves weapons for the battle (Eph 6:16), which is the preparation for the gospel.

6.10.11.en: Let us knock at the door of heaven (Mt 7:7), and it will be opened before us and we shall enter it.

6.10.12.en: Let us ask for mercy diligently, and we shall receive what is necessary for us. Let us seek His kingdom and His righteousness (Mt 6:33).

6.10.13.en: Let us meditate on what is above, on the heavenly things, where Christ is ascended and glorified.

6.10.14.en: But let us forget the world, which is not ours, until we reach the goal to which we are called.

6.10.15.en: Let us lift up our eyes to the heights to see the light that is manifested.

6.10.16.en: Let us lift up our wings like eagles, to see where the body is (Mt 24:28)...

6.10.17.en: Our enemy is clever, my dear, and he who fights us is a deceiver. He prepares himself to attack the courageous victors, to make them weak. But the feeble ones who are his he does not fight, for they are captives delivered up to him.

6.10.18.en: Whoever has two wings flies away from him with them, so that the arrows he hurls at him do not reach him. The spiritual see him fighting, and his weapon does not prevail over their bodies. All the children of light do not fear him, for darkness flees before the light. The children of the Good One do not fear the evil one, for He gave them to tread upon him with their feet (Gen 3:15).

6.10.19.en: St. Aphrahat Is my strength the strength of stones?

6.11.0.en: or is my flesh of brass? [12]

6.11.1.en: * [Is my strength the strength of stones? or is my flesh of brass?] (Job 6:12) Even if my strength were like the strength of stones or brass, the torments issuing from the enemy would make it give way, for he [esteemeth iron as straw, and brass as rotten wood] (Job 41:27). If God says this of the enemy, then it is necessary that we seek departure from this body on every side.

6.11.2.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * It is necessary to bear in mind that the "strength" of the righteous is of one kind, and the strength of the corrupt of another.

6.11.3.en: For the strength of the righteous is to subdue the body and resist our own will, and to destroy the pleasure of the present life, and to love the roughness of this world for the sake of eternal rewards, and to despise the enticements of prosperity, and to overcome the terror of trials in our hearts; but the strength of the corrupt is unbroken attachment to passing things, and continual demand for more vainglory, even at the cost of life, and the search for greater measures of evil, and the resisting of the life of the righteous, not only with words and conduct but also with arms, so that they may be self-assertive, and the committing of evil daily without any lessening of desire.

6.11.4.en: Therefore it was said to the elect by the psalmist: "Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all ye that wait for the LORD" (Ps 24:31). And it was proclaimed to the corrupt by the prophet: "Woe unto them that are mighty to drink wine, and men of strength to mingle strong drink" (Isa 22:5).

6.11.5.en: How well Isaiah perceived both kinds of strength in the words: "But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength" (Isa 31:40). For since he did not say "receive" but "change" (renew) strength, he clearly perceives that the strength they leave is of one kind and that which enters them is of another.

6.11.6.en: * What we indicate here by brass and stones, is it not the blows of the Most High, which have been softened by no blows of discipline? On the contrary, it was said to the elect by the prophet, with a promise from the Lord: "And I will take away the stony heart out of their flesh, and will give them an heart of flesh" (Ezek 19:11).

6.11.8.en: It was not possible for Job to rely on his own strength, but he places his hope in our Lord Jesus, the Giver of strength.

6.11.9.en: * Among all those born who put on flesh there is one who is righteous, He is Jesus Christ, as He testifies of Himself, saying: "I have overcome the world" (Jn 16:33). And the prophet also testified of Him: "Because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth" (Isa 53:9). And the blessed Apostle said: "For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin" (2 Cor 5:21). How did He make Him sin? He bore sin without committing it, and nailed it to the Cross (Col 2:14). The Apostle also says: "Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize?" (1 Cor 9:24).

6.11.10.en: Add to this that none among men went down to the battle and was not wounded or struck, because sin has ruled since Adam transgressed the commandment (Rom 5:14), striking many, wounding many, and killing many. And none among the many killed it until our Savior came on His cross. It had a sting that pricked many, until the end came, and its sting was broken when it was nailed to the Cross.

6.12.0.en: St. Aphrahat Verily my help is not in me, and succour is driven quite from me! [13]

6.12.1.en: * [There is no help for me from myself] [13]. Blessed Job was rich in virtue, yet he was not self-reliant, so he spoke thus as one without strength... It is clear now that, as one whose mind was struck with regard to hope, he looks that he has no hope from himself. But since he declares that he is weak in himself, he adds also that his kinsmen have forsaken him. [My friends also have left me]. But note that he who is despised from without sits within on the judgment seat. For at the very moment in which he declares himself abandoned, he immediately breaks that by uttering judgment in the words: [He that withholdeth pity from his friend forsaketh the fear of the Lord](a).

6.12.3.en: Job groaned over his friends because they left him in his trial, but our Lord, the glorious Jesus, did not leave man whom He loved, but crossed over to him even to Hades to free him from it.

6.12.4.en: * When Jesus, the slayer of death, came, and clothed Himself with a body from the seed of Adam, and was crucified in His body, and tasted death, and when Death realized that He had come to it, it was terrified in its place, and was confounded when it saw Jesus. It had shut its gates and did not wish to meet Him. Then He burst open its gates, and entered it and spoiled it of its plunder.

6.12.5.en: And when the dead saw a light in the darkness, they lifted up their heads from the bondage of death, and looked and saw the exaltation of the Messiah the King. Then the powers of darkness sat in mourning, for the authority of death had been taken from them.

6.12.6.en: Death tasted the deadly medicine for it, and its hands fell, and it learned that the dead would rise and flee from its authority. And when (Jesus) struck Death by despoiling its possessions, it wailed and cried aloud in bitterness, saying: "Get away from my kingdom, do not enter it. Who is this living One who enters my world?"

6.12.7.en: And as Death cried out in terror (for it saw the darkness beginning to vanish, and some of the righteous who slept arose to ascend with Him) it realized that when He comes in the fullness of time, He will bring out all those imprisoned under its authority, and they will go to see the light.

6.12.8.en: Therefore when Jesus completed His ministry among the dead, Death cast Him out of its kingdom, and did not permit Him to remain in it. And it reckoned that its devouring Him like the rest of the dead was not pleasing, for it has no authority over the Holy One, and corruption cannot come upon Him...

6.12.9.en: Just as when a man takes poison in the food given for life, and realizes in himself that he has eaten poison in the food, he vomits the food mixed with poison from his belly, but the effect of the poison remains working in his members, until the structure of the body dissolves little by little and corrupts. So the death of Jesus abolished death, for by it life reigns and death is abolished, he to whom it is said: [O death, where is thy victory?] (1 Cor 55:15).

6.13.s.en: 3. His criticism of his friends' harshness

6.13.0.en: 14 The right of the sorrowful is known from his friend, though he forsake the fear of the Almighty. 15 My brethren have dealt deceitfully as a brook, as the stream of brooks they pass away; 16 Which are turbid with hail, and the snow is hid in them. 17 When they flow, they are cut off; when they grow hot, they dry up out of their place. 18 The caravans turn aside from their way; they go into the waste, and perish. 19 The caravans of Tema looked, the travellers of Sheba hoped for it. 20 They were ashamed because they had been confident; they came thither, and were abashed. 21 For now ye are become like it; ye see a blow, and are afraid. 22 Did I say, Give me something, or from your substance bribe on my behalf? 23 Or, Deliver me from the hand of the adversary, or redeem me from the hand of the tyrants? 24 Teach me, and I will hold my peace: and cause me to understand wherein I have erred. 25 How forcible are upright words! but what doth your reproof prove? 26 Do ye think to reprove words, when the speech of one in despair is for the wind? 27 Nay, ye fall upon the fatherless, and dig a pit for your friend. 28 Now therefore look upon me; for I will not lie to your faces. 29 Return, let there be no injustice; return again, my right is in it. 30 Is there injustice in my tongue? or cannot my palate discern perverse things?

6.13.1.en: The right of the sorrowful is known from his friend, though he forsake the fear of the Almighty [14].

6.13.2.en: Job rebukes his friends for their violence and harshness. Truly only Eliphaz spoke, but signs of acceptance and agreement appeared from the other two friends. Job feels that their harshness has become a new reason to wish for death, for what rest has he in this world if his friends who came to console him have become his tormentors?

6.13.3.en: It is the right of the sorrowing man that those who are at ease should show him sympathy, and display pure love to him, and cheer his heart, and listen to his complaint, and mingle his tears with their tears. This is what is fitting for them as members with the sorrowing one in the same one body.

6.13.4.en: He who does not show tenderness to the sufferer has forsaken the fear of the Almighty, that is, has lost the fear of the Lord, for how can the love of the Lord and His fear be established in one who does not care about the pains of his brother (1 Jn 3:17)?

6.13.5.en: Are trials the touchstone of friendship? They reveal true friends from those who claim friendship. [A brother is born for adversity] (Prov 17:17).

6.13.6.en: * There are two commandments of love: the love of God and the love of our neighbor. By the love of God the love of neighbor comes into being. And by the love of neighbor the love of God is strengthened. For he who truly does not care for the love of God knows nothing of how to love his neighbor, and when we advance in greater perfection in the love of God we suckle the milk of love toward our neighbor.

6.13.7.en: Because the love of God begets the love of neighbor, therefore when the Lord spoke with the voice of the Law and uttered the words "Thou shalt love thy neighbour," it was preceded by His saying: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God" (Mt 37:22; Deut 5:6, 10, 12)... Again the love of God is strengthened by love of our neighbor, and John testified to this, saying: "He that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?" (1 Jn 20:4)... By this a wise man rightly says: [A friend cannot be known in prosperity: and an enemy cannot be hid in adversity] (Sir 8:12).

6.13.9.en: * It is not enough to show mercy, but it is fitting for us to give it generously, with a bountiful spirit, and not only a bountiful spirit but a joyful, cheerful spirit...

6.13.10.en: And he stressed the same point strongly when he wrote to the Corinthians to urge them to generosity, saying: "He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully" (2 Cor 9:6). And to correct their disposition he says: "Not grudgingly, or of necessity" (2 Cor 9:7)... For if you grieve while you do mercy, you are harsh and violent.

6.13.11.en: If you are sad, how can you support those who are in sorrow...? This is the reason for saying "he that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness," for how can he who receives the Kingdom be sad of countenance?! Who remains gloomy of look while receiving the forgiveness of his sins? Therefore do not think of your spending of money (work of mercy), but of the overflow you receive through the spending. For if he who sows rejoices though he sows uncertain as to the harvest, how much more he who ploughs the heavens? For you give only little to receive much... By two mites the widow was reckoned to have surpassed those who offered many talents, and this because of her generous spirit.

6.13.12.en: * The strong is joined to the weak and supports him, and does not allow his perishing.

6.13.13.en: Again if he is joined to a slothful person he raises him up and urges him to work. It is said: "A brother helped by a brother is as a strong city." This is not surpassed by distance of space, nor heaven, nor earth, nor death, nor any other thing, but it is stronger and more effective than all things. This, though it proceeds from one soul, is able to embrace many at once.

6.13.14.en: Hear what Paul says: "Ye are not straitened in us, but ye are straitened in your own bowels... be ye also enlarged."

6.13.15.en: St. John Chrysostom * "A faithful friend is the medicine of life" (Sir 6:16).

6.13.16.en: There is no remedy as effective in healing pains as the sincere friend who comforts you in your afflictions, and manages you in your troubles, and rejoices in your success, and grieves in your calamities. He who has found such a friend has found a treasure. For the faithful friend has no equal, and the weight of gold and silver does not equal the goodness of his faithfulness (see Sir 6:14-15).

6.13.17.en: * Rightly may you have a friend whom you call "half of my soul."

6.13.18.en: * There is no true friendship unless you make it like a joint that welds souls, so they cleave together by the love poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit.

6.13.19.en: * There is no remedy as effective for healing pains as the sincere friend who comforts you in your afflictions.

6.14.0.en: St. Augustine My brethren have dealt deceitfully as a brook, as the stream of brooks they pass away [15].

6.14.1.en: When they came together to console him, and remained seven days and seven nights silent, he expected from them a word of consolation that would quench the inner flame, but they pounced on him savagely like those who betray him, heaping false accusations on him, and pouring on his wound what inflames it, instead of offering oil to soothe its inflammation.

6.14.2.en: * [My nearest acquaintances did not support my needs]. Merely because God ignored him, his relatives made light of him amid such pains. For every time God draws away, man is deprived of his refuge, and all become against him as enemies. He says no one knew me in my trial. But this is in the seriousness that [all who used to honor me are now against me](c). It is exceedingly bad that a person should trample under his feet a man lying prostrate. It seems to me that he was alluding by this to his friends who were with him.

6.14.3.en: * Had he not been wicked he would not have become your enemy. So desire good for him, and his evil will end, and he will no longer be your enemy. He is your enemy not because of his human nature but because of his sin!

6.14.4.en: St. John Chrysostom Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that Job likens his friends to those who fear the ice that freezes from below and the snow falling upon them from above. They trample with their feet on those on whom temporal earthly trials have come, since they seek the glory of the world, and they do not realize that heavenly punishment will come upon them like snow falling upon them, from which they cannot escape.
